chapter.name: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures

questions.q: What name does the chapter give to the individual substances that make up a mixture?
questions.a: Components

questions.q: Which gas makes up about 78% of the air and does not take part in combustion?
questions.a: Nitrogen

questions.q: Meera's school prize table has a brass bell, a bronze medal and a stainless steel plate. Which metal is present in both the brass bell and the bronze medal, but is not one of the substances the chapter lists for stainless steel?
questions.a: Copper

questions.q:
Read these statements about mixtures.
I. Stainless steel looks the same throughout, so it must be a compound and not a mixture.
II. Lemonade is a mixture, so the lemon juice in it keeps its own properties.
III. A sprout salad and sugar dissolved in water are both mixtures, but only the sprout salad is non-uniform.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Air is a uniform mixture.
Reason (R): Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'In a mixture, the components react chemically with each other and form a new substance.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The components of a mixture do not react chemically with each other; each substance in a mixture keeps (retains) its own properties.
s: States False
Corrects it: the components do not react chemically and each keeps its own properties

questions.q: (a) What is a uniform mixture? (b) Give one example of a uniform mixture from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A uniform mixture is one in which the components are evenly distributed and cannot be distinguished, even with the help of a microscope. (b) Sugar dissolved in water (air or stainless steel are also accepted).
s: (a) Says the components are evenly spread and cannot be told apart even under a microscope
(b) Gives sugar dissolved in water, air or stainless steel

questions.q: Kunal says, 'Air is a uniform mixture, so the air in every place and at every time must carry exactly the same things, including the same dust.' What is right and what is wrong in his statement? Explain using what the chapter says about the gases of air and about dust.
questions.a: Right: air is indeed a uniform mixture of mainly nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Wrong: dust is not an integral part of the air. Dust particles are only suspended in it and are counted as pollutants, and the nature and number of dust particles vary from time to time and from place to place. So the dust need not be the same everywhere.
s: Says the right part: air is a uniform mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour
Says the wrong part: dust is suspended in air and is a pollutant, not an integral part of air
States that the nature and number of dust particles vary with time and place, so the dust need not be the same

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Shillong sets up a 'mixture corner' with four exhibits. Exhibit 1 is a bowl of bhel puri in which puffed rice, peanuts, onion and sev can all be seen. Exhibit 2 is a glass of sugar syrup in which no separate sugar can be seen even under the school microscope. Exhibit 3 is a stainless steel tiffin box. Exhibit 4 is a petri dish of clear lime water that was left open on the lab bench and turned milky after four hours.
(a) Which exhibit is a non-uniform mixture?
(b) Is the sugar syrup a uniform or a non-uniform mixture? Give the reason.
(c) Name the four substances that make up the tiffin box metal.
(d) Which gas from the air turned the lime water milky, and what white substance was formed?
questions.a: (a) Exhibit 1, the bhel puri, because its components can be seen with the naked eye. (b) Uniform, because its components are evenly spread and cannot be told apart even under a microscope. (c) Iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon. (d) Carbon dioxide; it reacts with the calcium hydroxide in lime water to form calcium carbonate (insoluble tiny white particles) and water.
s: (a) Names the bhel puri, whose parts can be seen
(b) Says uniform, as nothing separate is seen even under a microscope
(c) Names iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon
(d) Names carbon dioxide and calcium carbonate

questions.q:
A teacher in Bhopal has four gases, labelled J1 to J4: one is room air, one only nitrogen, one only oxygen and one only carbon dioxide. She fills two sealed jars with each gas. Into one jar of each gas she puts a burning splinter; in the other jar of each gas she leaves clear lime water for a few hours. Results: J1: the splinter goes out; the lime water stays clear. J2: the splinter glows brighter; the lime water stays clear. J3: the splinter keeps burning for a while; the lime water turns milky. J4: the splinter goes out; the lime water turns milky.
(a) Which gas is only nitrogen? Give the two results that settle it.
(b) Which gas is only oxygen? Give the reason.
(c) Which gas is room air? Explain why it cannot be the gas that is only oxygen or the gas that is only carbon dioxide.
(d) Which of the four gases are pure substances and which is a mixture?
(e) A student says, 'J3 must be a compound, because one gas cannot both help burning and turn lime water milky.' Evaluate her claim.
questions.a: (a) J1. The splinter goes out, as nitrogen does not take part in combustion, and the lime water stays clear, so there is no carbon dioxide. (b) J2. The splinter glows brighter, as oxygen helps combustion, and the lime water stays clear, so there is no carbon dioxide. (c) J3. The splinter keeps burning, so it has oxygen, and the lime water turns milky, so it also has carbon dioxide; the oxygen (J2) shows no carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide (J4) does not keep the splinter burning. (d) J1 (nitrogen), J2 (oxygen) and J4 (carbon dioxide) are pure substances; J3 (air) is a mixture. (e) The claim is wrong. Air is a mixture of gases, and in a mixture each component keeps its own properties: the oxygen in it still helps burning and the carbon dioxide in it still turns lime water milky. Showing the properties of two different gases is a sign of a mixture, not of a compound.
s: (a) Names J1, using the splinter going out and the lime water staying clear
(b) Names J2, because the splinter glows brighter and there is no carbon dioxide
(c) Names J3, as it shows both oxygen (splinter burns) and carbon dioxide (milky lime water)
(d) Says J1, J2 and J4 are pure substances and J3 is a mixture
(e) Rejects the claim: in the mixture air, oxygen and carbon dioxide each keep their own properties

questions.q: In common usage, what does the word 'pure' printed on a packet of ghee mean?
questions.a: Nothing cheaper or of poor quality has been added to it
o: Nothing cheaper or of poor quality has been added to it
It is made of only one type of particle throughout the packet
It cannot be separated by any physical process
It contains atoms of only one element

questions.q: When a scientist says that a substance is pure, what does she mean?
questions.a: The substance consists of the same type of particles
o: The substance consists of the same type of particles
The substance looks the same throughout to the naked eye
The substance has no added colour or flavour
The substance comes from natural sources only

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: I. Adulteration  II. 'Pure' in common usage  III. Pure substance in science  IV. Component
Column II: A. Has no other substance present in it and consists of the same type of particles  B. Unadulterated  C. Illegally adding cheaper or poor-quality substances to a product  D. One of the individual substances that make up a mixture
questions.a: I-C, II-B, III-A, IV-D

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Adulteration can make a product hazardous to health.
Reason (R): Adulteration is usually done to improve the quality of a product.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A pure substance cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A pure substance has no other substance present in it; it consists of the same type of particles, so there are no other kinds of matter in it to separate out by a physical process.
s: States True
Explains that it has no other substance in it and consists of one type of particle

questions.q: (a) What is adulteration? (b) State one reason why it is usually done.
questions.a: (a) Adulteration is the illegal process of adding substances which are cheaper, or of a poor quality, to a product. (b) It is usually done to increase the quantity of the product or to reduce the manufacturing cost.
s: (a) Defines adulteration as illegally adding cheaper or poor-quality substances
(b) Gives increasing the quantity or reducing the manufacturing cost

questions.q: A jar labelled 'pure honey' is tested by a food lab, which finds that cheap sugar syrup has been added to it to increase the quantity. (a) Is the label correct in the common-usage sense of 'pure'? Give the reason. (b) Would a scientist call the contents of the jar a pure substance? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) No. Adding a cheaper substance to increase the quantity is adulteration, so the honey is not unadulterated, which is what 'pure' means in common usage. (b) No. The jar holds more than one substance (the honey and the added sugar syrup), so it does not consist of the same type of particles.
s: (a) Says no, because adding cheap syrup to increase quantity is adulteration
(b) Says no, because the jar holds more than one substance

questions.q: Sana says, 'If a sample looks exactly the same all through, even under a microscope, it must be a pure substance.' Test her claim using one example from the chapter, and state what actually decides whether a substance is pure.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong. Sugar dissolved in water looks the same all through and its sugar and water particles cannot be seen separately even under a microscope, yet it is a uniform mixture of two substances, not a pure substance. What decides purity is whether the substance consists of the same type of particles, with no other substance present in it, not how it looks.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Gives a uniform mixture such as sugar dissolved in water that looks the same under a microscope but has two substances
States that a pure substance must have only one type of particle and no other substance present

questions.q: In the scientific sense, say whether each of these is a pure substance or not, and give the reason in a few words. (a) The oxygen gas collected when electric current is passed through acidified water. (b) Sugar dissolved in water. (c) A sprout salad.
questions.a: (a) Pure substance: oxygen is an element and consists of the same type of particles. (b) Not pure: it is a mixture of two substances, sugar and water. (c) Not pure: it is a mixture of several substances such as green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato.
s: (a) Pure, because oxygen has one type of particle
(b) Not pure, a mixture of sugar and water
(c) Not pure, a mixture of several components

questions.q: A consumer club in Lucknow tests three products, each sold with the word 'pure' on the packet. Product X is chilli powder; the lab finds brick powder mixed into it to add weight. Product Y is common salt; the lab finds nothing added and only one substance, sodium chloride, in it. Product Z is a masala of eight ground spices; the lab finds nothing cheaper added. (a) Which product is adulterated? (b) Which product is pure in both the common-usage and the scientific sense? (c) Which product is pure in common usage but not in science? (d) The club can file only one complaint with the food authorities. Which product should it report, and why?
questions.a: (a) Product X, the chilli powder, because a cheaper substance (brick powder) was added to increase the quantity. (b) Product Y, the salt: it is unadulterated and it is a single substance with one type of particle. (c) Product Z: nothing cheaper was added, so it is pure in common usage, but it is made of more than one substance, so it is not pure in science. (d) Product X: adulteration is illegal and can make the product hazardous to health, whereas Product Z being a mixture of spices is not wrong at all; it is only 'impure' in the scientific sense.
s: (a) Names Product X as adulterated
(b) Names Product Y as pure in both senses
(c) Names Product Z, explaining it is unadulterated but made of more than one substance
(d) Reports Product X because adulteration is illegal and can harm health, while Z is only scientifically impure

questions.q: What are the identical particles that make up an element called?
questions.a: Atoms

questions.q: According to the chapter, how many atoms of hydrogen combine to form one molecule of hydrogen?
questions.a: Two

questions.q: A scientist heats a new white solid strongly. It gives off a gas and leaves behind a different solid. What can she correctly conclude about the white solid?
questions.a: It is not an element, because it has been broken down into simpler substances
o: It is not an element, because it has been broken down into simpler substances
It is an element, because it was a single white solid to begin with
It is an element, because it is made of atoms
It must be a mixture, because a gas came out of it

questions.q:
Read these statements about water and its constituents.
I. The gases collected when electric current is passed through acidified water are not water vapour, since water vapour would have condensed back to form water.
II. Hydrogen and oxygen can be broken down further into simpler substances.
III. When water is frozen into ice and melted again, its particles change into hydrogen and oxygen.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hydrogen gas is made of molecules, not of single separate atoms.
Reason (R): The atoms of most elements cannot exist independently, so two or more of them combine to form a stable particle called a molecule.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Define an element. (b) Name two elements from the chapter other than hydrogen and oxygen.
questions.a: (a) An element is a pure substance made up of identical particles called atoms, which cannot be broken down further into simpler substances. (b) Any two of gold, silver, sulfur and carbon.
s: (a) Defines an element as made of identical atoms and not breakable into simpler substances
(b) Names two of gold, silver, sulfur and carbon

questions.q: Water can be frozen into ice and the ice melted back into water. Water can also have electric current passed through it after a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid are added. (a) In which process do the particles of water remain the same? (b) Which process shows that water is made of two different constituents, and what are they?
questions.a: (a) Freezing water into ice and melting it back: the particles of water remain the same. (b) Passing electric current through the acidified water; it shows that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
s: (a) Names freezing and melting as the process in which water particles stay the same
(b) Names passing electric current and gives hydrogen and oxygen

questions.q: In the demonstration of passing electric current through acidified water, a burning candle is brought near the mouth of each test tube of gas. (a) Name the gas that gives a pop sound. (b) Name the gas that makes the flame glow brighter. (c) Write the word equation for what happens to the water.
questions.a: (a) Hydrogen. (b) Oxygen. (c) Water gives Hydrogen + Oxygen.
s: (a) Names hydrogen for the pop sound
(b) Names oxygen for the brighter flame
(c) Writes Water gives Hydrogen + Oxygen

questions.q: A teacher shows a cylinder of oxygen gas and says it holds an element. Ramesh objects: 'Each particle of this gas is two atoms joined together, and anything made by joining atoms is a compound.' (a) What is the joined particle of oxygen gas called? (b) Is Ramesh right? Give the reason. (c) State what must be true for a substance to be a compound.
questions.a: (a) A molecule of oxygen. (b) No. Both atoms in an oxygen molecule are identical oxygen atoms, so the gas is still made of only one kind of atom and is an element. (c) A compound is formed only when different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio, giving something entirely new with different properties.
s: (a) Names the particle a molecule
(b) Says Ramesh is wrong because both atoms are the same kind, so oxygen is an element
(c) States that a compound needs different elements combined in a fixed ratio

questions.q:
At a science quiz in Jaipur, four sealed cylinders carry these lab cards. Cylinder 1: only hydrogen molecules, 5,000 of them. Cylinder 2: only oxygen molecules. Cylinder 3: pure water. Cylinder 4: air from the hall. Each molecule of hydrogen and oxygen is formed the way the chapter describes.
(a) Which cylinders hold only a single element?
(b) How many hydrogen atoms are in Cylinder 1?
(c) The content of which cylinder can be broken down by passing electric current into the gases of Cylinders 1 and 2?
(d) The quizmaster says, 'The elements in Cylinders 1 and 2 are enough to make up everything in Cylinder 3, but not everything in Cylinder 4.' Is this right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Cylinders 1 and 2: Cylinder 1 holds only hydrogen and Cylinder 2 only oxygen. (Air in Cylinder 4 contains oxygen and nitrogen, but as a mixture of several substances.) (b) 5,000 x 2 = 10,000 hydrogen atoms. (c) Cylinder 3, water, which gives hydrogen and oxygen. (d) Yes. Water is made only of the elements hydrogen and oxygen, but air is a mixture of mainly nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour, so it also contains substances such as nitrogen and argon that are not made of hydrogen and oxygen.
s: (a) Names Cylinders 1 and 2 as holding only a single element each
(b) Finds 10,000 hydrogen atoms
(c) Names Cylinder 3, water
(d) Agrees, using water = hydrogen + oxygen and air containing nitrogen and argon too

questions.q: What is the ratio of the number of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms in water?
A tiny drop of pure water is made of 2,700 atoms in all. How many of these atoms are hydrogen atoms?

Match each compound in Column I with the elements it is made of in Column II.
Column I: I. Water  II. Common salt (sodium chloride)  III. Sugar  IV. Iron sulfide
Column II: A. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen  B. Iron and sulfur  C. Hydrogen and oxygen  D. Sodium and chlorine
questions.a: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sugar is an element, because it is a single white substance.
Reason (R): On heating, sugar gives carbon and water.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: True or False? 'The properties of a compound are the same as the properties of the elements that form it.' Give the verdict and a reason with an example from the chapter.
questions.a: False. The properties of a compound are different from those of its elements. For example, sodium is a soft metal and chlorine is a hazardous gas, but the compound they form, sodium chloride (common salt), is harmless and enhances taste.
s: States False
Gives an example such as sodium and chlorine forming harmless common salt

questions.q: Anu heats iron filings and sulfur powder together until a black mass forms, which is then ground to a powder. A magnet moved over the powder picks up nothing. (a) Name the black powder. (b) Her friend says, 'The magnet picks up nothing because the iron burnt away during heating.' Give the correct reason.
questions.a: (a) Iron sulfide. (b) The iron did not burn away: it combined chemically with the sulfur to form iron sulfide, a new substance with completely different properties, and iron sulfide is not attracted by a magnet. The iron and sulfur can no longer be separated.
s: (a) Names iron sulfide
(b) Explains that the iron combined with sulfur into a new substance with different properties, not attracted by a magnet

questions.q: (a) Define a compound. (b) Give one example of a compound from the chapter and name the elements in it. (c) Can the elements of a compound be separated by physical methods?
questions.a: (a) A compound is formed when different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio to form something entirely new, with properties different from its elements. (b) Water, made of hydrogen and oxygen (or sodium chloride, made of sodium and chlorine). (c) No. The constituent elements of a compound cannot be separated by any physical method.
s: (a) Defines a compound as different elements combined in a fixed ratio
(b) Gives a compound with its elements, such as water: hydrogen and oxygen
(c) Says no physical method can separate them

questions.q: Ritu says, 'Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, so if I simply put hydrogen gas and oxygen gas into a jar in any amounts, the jar will hold water.' Explain what is correct in her statement and what is wrong, using what the chapter says about mixtures and compounds.
questions.a: Correct: water is indeed made of the elements hydrogen and oxygen. Wrong: gases simply put together in a jar form a mixture, in which each gas keeps its own properties and does not react. Also wrong: in water, hydrogen and oxygen are combined chemically in a fixed ratio of 2 hydrogen atoms to 1 oxygen atom, forming an entirely new substance; gases put together in 'any amounts' do not give this.
s: States the correct part: water is made of hydrogen and oxygen
Explains that gases simply put together form a mixture whose parts keep their properties
Explains that water needs chemical combination in the fixed 2:1 ratio, so any amounts will not do

questions.q:
A salt works near Thoothukudi lets salt water stand in shallow pans in the sun until the water evaporates and white common salt is left. A lab report on one small sample of this salt says that it is pure sodium chloride. The company is preparing a new packet design.
(a) Name the two elements in common salt and give the ratio in which their particles are present.
(b) Sodium is a soft metal and chlorine is a hazardous gas. How are the properties of common salt different from these?
(c) Evaporation separated the salt from the water. Did it also separate the salt into its elements? Give the reason.
(d) The designer wants the packet to say, 'A mixture of sodium and chlorine.' Should the company print this? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Sodium and chlorine, in a 1:1 ratio. (b) Common salt is harmless and taste-enhancing, and essential for our lives; the properties of a compound are different from those of the elements forming it. (c) No. Evaporation is a physical process; it separates dissolved salt from water, but the elements of a compound cannot be separated by any physical method. (d) No. Common salt is a compound, not a mixture: sodium and chlorine are combined chemically in a fixed 1:1 ratio, and they cannot be separated by physical means.
s: (a) Names sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio
(b) Says salt is harmless and taste-enhancing, unlike soft sodium and hazardous chlorine
(c) Says no, since evaporation is physical and cannot split a compound
(d) Rejects the wording, using the fixed 1:1 ratio and that the elements cannot be separated physically

questions.q:
A teacher gives two samples, P and Q, both made from the same iron filings and sulfur powder. Sample P shows black and yellow specks; a magnet picks up the black specks; with dilute hydrochloric acid it gives a colourless, odourless gas that burns with a pop, and a yellow solid is left. Sample Q is a black mass of the same colour and texture throughout; a magnet has no effect; with dilute hydrochloric acid it gives a colourless gas that smells of rotten eggs.
(a) Which sample is a mixture and which is a compound? Name the compound.
(b) Write the word equation for the reaction of the iron in P with dilute hydrochloric acid.
(c) Write the word equation for the reaction of Q with dilute hydrochloric acid.
(d) Explain why the magnet attracts something in P but nothing in Q.
(e) A student says, 'Q is only P ground into a finer powder.' Evaluate this claim using two observations from the data.
questions.a: (a) P is a mixture of iron and sulfur; Q is a compound, iron sulfide. (b) Iron + Dilute hydrochloric acid gives Iron chloride + Hydrogen gas. (c) Iron sulfide + Dilute hydrochloric acid gives Iron chloride + Hydrogen sulfide. (d) In the mixture P, the iron keeps its own properties, so the iron filings are attracted by the magnet; in Q the iron has combined with sulfur to form a new substance with completely different properties, which is not attracted by a magnet. (e) The claim is wrong. If Q were only a finer form of P, its iron and sulfur would still keep their own properties, but Q behaves differently: a magnet has no effect on it, and with the acid it gives a gas that smells of rotten eggs (hydrogen sulfide) instead of odourless hydrogen. It also shows no yellow specks. So Q is a new substance, a compound, not a finer mixture.
s: (a) Says P is a mixture and Q is the compound iron sulfide
(b) Writes Iron + dilute hydrochloric acid gives iron chloride + hydrogen
(c) Writes Iron sulfide + dilute hydrochloric acid gives iron chloride + hydrogen sulfide
(d) Explains that iron keeps its properties in P but not in the compound Q
(e) Rejects the claim using two differences, such as the magnet test and the gas odour

questions.q: Which material does the chapter describe as stronger and more durable than pure iron?
questions.a: Stainless steel

questions.q: Which list contains only building materials that the chapter calls mixtures?
questions.a: Wood, steel and concrete

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with the description in Column II that fits it.
Column I: I. Iron  II. Water  III. Air  IV. Fertilisers
Column II: A. A mixture of gases that we breathe  B. Made with chemists' knowledge of how elements combine, and enhances crop production  C. An element used to construct bridges, buildings and vehicles  D. A compound of hydrogen and oxygen that is essential for life
questions.a: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B

questions.q: (a) Chemists study how elements combine to create compounds. Name two things this lets them invent to fight diseases. (b) How does the same knowledge help to feed the growing human population?
questions.a: (a) Life-saving medicines and vaccines. (b) It helps in creating fertilisers, which enhance crop production.
s: (a) Names medicines and vaccines
(b) Says it helps make fertilisers that enhance crop production

questions.q: A material scientist mixes copper and tin so evenly that the two metals can no longer be seen separately, and each keeps its own properties without reacting. (a) Is the new material an element, a compound or a mixture, and is it uniform or non-uniform? (b) Which alloy named in the chapter is made of these same two metals?
questions.a: (a) It is a mixture, because the metals keep their own properties and do not react; it is uniform, because the metals cannot be seen separately. Such a uniform mixture of metals is an alloy. (b) Bronze.
s: (a) Says mixture and uniform, with the reason
(b) Names bronze

questions.q: Engineers need railings for a railway station that are stronger and last longer than railings of pure iron. Which approach, described in the chapter, have material scientists used to get such a material?
questions.a: Mixing iron evenly with nickel, chromium and a little carbon to make an alloy
o: Mixing iron evenly with nickel, chromium and a little carbon to make an alloy
Heating iron with sulfur so that it turns into a new compound
Breaking iron down into simpler substances that are stronger
Purifying the iron further so that it holds only one kind of particle

questions.q: Gopal says, 'Only compounds are useful to people. Elements and mixtures are just raw materials that nobody uses as they are.' Test his claim with one example of a useful element and two examples of useful mixtures from the chapter.
questions.a: His claim is wrong. Elements are used as they are: iron and aluminium are used to construct bridges, buildings and vehicles. Mixtures are useful too: the air we breathe is a mixture of gases, stainless steel is an alloy (a mixture) that is stronger and more durable than pure iron, and wood, steel and concrete used as building materials are all mixtures.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Gives a useful element, such as iron or aluminium for bridges and vehicles
Gives two useful mixtures, such as air, stainless steel, wood or concrete

questions.q: A farmers' cooperative in Punjab grows wheat on 10 acres and must use one fertiliser on all of them. Two fertilisers are offered (illustrative figures). Fertiliser P costs Rs 1,200 per acre and raises the wheat yield by 300 kg per acre. Fertiliser Q costs Rs 2,000 per acre and raises the yield by 400 kg per acre. Wheat sells at Rs 20 per kg, and the cooperative has Rs 25,000 to spend on fertiliser. (a) Which knowledge of chemists makes fertilisers possible, and how do fertilisers help to feed people? (b) For each fertiliser, find the extra money earned per acre after paying for the fertiliser. (c) Find the cost of each fertiliser for all 10 acres. (d) Which fertiliser should the cooperative choose? Justify using your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Chemists study how elements combine to create compounds; this knowledge helps in creating fertilisers, which enhance crop production and so help feed the growing population. (b) P: 300 x 20 = Rs 6,000 of extra wheat, minus Rs 1,200 = Rs 4,800 per acre. Q: 400 x 20 = Rs 8,000, minus Rs 2,000 = Rs 6,000 per acre. (c) P: 1,200 x 10 = Rs 12,000. Q: 2,000 x 10 = Rs 20,000. (d) Fertiliser Q. Both fit the Rs 25,000 budget (Rs 12,000 and Rs 20,000), so the choice is settled by what each earns: Q earns Rs 6,000 per acre against Rs 4,800 for P, that is Rs 60,000 against Rs 48,000 over the 10 acres, even though it costs more.
s: (a) Names the knowledge of how elements combine into compounds, and fertilisers enhancing crop production
(b) Finds Rs 4,800 per acre for P and Rs 6,000 per acre for Q
(c) Finds Rs 12,000 for P and Rs 20,000 for Q
(d) Chooses Q: both fit the Rs 25,000 budget and Q earns more per acre (Rs 6,000 against Rs 4,800)

questions.q: Say whether each of these things in Ravi's house is an element, a compound or a mixture, and give one reason for each. (a) An aluminium ladder. (b) Distilled water, with nothing dissolved in it. (c) A wooden table. (d) A stainless steel spoon. (e) The air in his room.
questions.a: (a) Element: aluminium is an element, made of one kind of atom. (b) Compound: distilled water is only the substance water, made of hydrogen and oxygen combined in a fixed ratio. (c) Mixture: the chapter says wood is a mixture. (d) Mixture: stainless steel is an alloy of iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon. (e) Mixture: air is a uniform mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
s: (a) Element, with the reason
(b) Compound of hydrogen and oxygen
(c) Mixture, as the chapter says of wood
(d) Mixture, an alloy of iron, nickel, chromium and carbon
(e) Mixture of gases

questions.q:
A medicines laboratory in Hyderabad makes a new compound M by combining two elements, X and Y. In compound M, the particles of X and Y are always combined in a fixed 1:2 ratio (illustrative figures). Two trial batches are checked. Batch 1: 4,000 particles of X and 8,000 particles of Y, all combined into M. Batch 2: 4,000 particles of X and 9,500 particles of Y; the Y that could not combine is still there as the element, with its own properties.
(a) Which knowledge of chemists makes such new medicines possible, and what does the chapter say this knowledge lets them invent to fight diseases?
(b) In Batch 2, how many particles of Y can combine with the 4,000 particles of X, and how many are left over?
(c) Is Batch 2 a pure substance or a mixture? Give the reason.
(d) Batch 1 also contains the element Y, yet it does not show the properties of Y. Explain why.
(e) Only a batch that is a pure substance may be sent for testing. Which batch should be sent? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Chemists study how elements combine to create compounds; this lets them invent life-saving medicines and vaccines to fight diseases. (b) X and Y combine in a 1:2 ratio, so 4,000 x 2 = 8,000 particles of Y combine, and 9,500 - 8,000 = 1,500 particles of Y are left over. (c) A mixture. It holds two substances, compound M and the left-over element Y, which keeps its own properties; a pure substance has no other substance present in it and consists of the same type of particles. (d) In Batch 1, Y is combined chemically with X in compound M, and the properties of a compound are different from those of the elements forming it. (e) Batch 1. Its 4,000 particles of X and 8,000 particles of Y are exactly in the 1:2 ratio, so all of them are combined and only compound M is present: it is a pure substance. Batch 2 has 1,500 particles of Y left over, so it is a mixture.
s: (a) Names the knowledge of how elements combine into compounds, and medicines and vaccines
(b) Finds 8,000 particles of Y combined and 1,500 left over
(c) Says mixture, as it holds compound M and left-over Y, not only one substance
(d) Explains that in a compound the properties differ from those of its elements
(e) Chooses Batch 1, as 4,000 : 8,000 is exactly 1:2 so only M is present, while Batch 2 has Y left over

questions.q: Which of these is a native mineral, that is, a mineral that is a pure element?
questions.a: Gold

questions.q: Talcum powder is made from which mineral?
questions.a: Talc

questions.q:
Read these statements about minerals.
I. A mineral has a fixed chemical composition, so in a mineral that is a compound the elements are always combined in the same ratio.
II. A mineral that is a compound can be split into its elements by grinding it into a very fine powder.
III. A solid made in a factory is not a mineral, even if it has a fixed make-up.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: True or False? 'A mineral can be a pure element, but most minerals are compounds.' Give the verdict and a reason with one example of each kind.
questions.a: True. Native minerals such as gold, silver, copper, sulfur and carbon are pure elements, but most minerals, such as quartz, calcite and mica, are compounds made up of more than one element.
s: States True
Gives a native mineral that is an element and a mineral that is a compound

questions.q: (a) What is a native mineral? (b) Name one native mineral that is a metal and one that is a non-metal.
questions.a: (a) A native mineral is a mineral that is a pure element and not a compound. (b) Metal: gold, silver or copper. Non-metal: sulfur or carbon.
s: (a) Defines a native mineral as a pure element, not a compound
(b) Names one metal (gold, silver or copper) and one non-metal (sulfur or carbon)

questions.q: Priya says, 'Oxygen is found naturally on the Earth and it is a pure element, so it is a native mineral, just like sulfur.' What is right and what is wrong in her statement? Explain using what the chapter says a mineral is.
questions.a: Right: oxygen is an element, a pure substance made of identical atoms, and it is found naturally, for example as one of the gases of air. Wrong: minerals are natural, solid substances found on the Earth with a fixed chemical composition. Oxygen is a gas, not a solid, so it is not a mineral at all, and so it cannot be a native mineral. Sulfur is different: it is found naturally as a solid that is a pure element, so it is a native mineral.
s: Says the right part: oxygen is an element and is found naturally, as in air
Says the wrong part: a mineral must be a solid, and oxygen is a gas, so it is not a mineral
Explains that sulfur is a native mineral because it is a natural solid that is a pure element

questions.q: (a) What are most rocks made of? (b) Name two minerals that are compounds. (c) Name the substances from which cement is made.
questions.a: (a) Most rocks are a mixture of minerals. (b) Any two of quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene and olivine. (c) Calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide.
s: (a) Says a mixture of minerals
(b) Names two of quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene and olivine
(c) Names calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide

questions.q:
A geology club in Dehradun breaks two pieces off the same boulder and, using a magnifying glass, sorts the grains of each piece by hand (illustrative figures). Piece 1 (200 g): quartz 110 g, mica 50 g, olivine 40 g. Piece 2 (250 g): quartz 100 g, mica 100 g, olivine 50 g. A lab finds that the quartz grains from both pieces have their elements combined in the same ratio.
(a) Find the percentage of quartz by mass in each piece.
(b) The grains could be told apart and sorted by hand. What does this show about the boulder?
(c) Why do the quartz grains from both pieces show the same ratio of elements?
(d) The club can put only one label on the boulder: Label A, 'Quartz: a mineral', or Label B, 'A rock: a mixture of the minerals quartz, mica and olivine'. Which label should it use? Justify using the data.
questions.a: (a) Piece 1: 110 / 200 x 100 = 55%. Piece 2: 100 / 250 x 100 = 40%. (b) Its components can be seen with a magnifying glass and separated by a physical process, so the boulder is not a pure substance but a non-uniform mixture of minerals, as most rocks are. (c) Quartz is a mineral, and a mineral has a fixed chemical composition: quartz is a compound whose elements are combined in a fixed ratio, so every sample of it has the same ratio. (d) Label B. The boulder holds three different minerals, and their shares change from piece to piece (quartz is 55% of one piece but only 40% of the other), so the boulder has no fixed chemical composition and cannot be a mineral. Quartz is only one of the minerals in it.
s: (a) Finds 55% for Piece 1 and 40% for Piece 2
(b) Says the boulder is a mixture of minerals, as its parts can be seen and separated physically
(c) Says quartz is a mineral with a fixed chemical composition, its elements combined in a fixed ratio
(d) Chooses Label B, using the changing quartz share (55% against 40%) to show there is no fixed composition

questions.q:
In a mine in Rajasthan, a team finds small lumps that a lab shows are made only of silver atoms. A silversmith in Cuttack buys 45 g of these lumps and mixes them evenly with 15 g of copper, each metal keeping its own properties, to make an ornament in which neither metal can be seen separately. A geology museum is collecting specimens for a display titled 'Minerals of India'.
(a) Is a lump an element, a compound or a mixture, and what kind of mineral is it?
(b) What percentage of the ornament's mass is silver?
(c) Is the ornament an element, a compound or a mixture? Give the reason.
(d) The silversmith offers the museum the ornament as a 'mineral specimen'. Should the museum accept it for this display? Justify using what a mineral is.
questions.a: (a) An element (silver); it is a native mineral, a mineral that is a pure element. (b) 45 / (45 + 15) x 100 = 75%. (c) A mixture: silver and copper are mixed evenly, each keeping its own properties, and are not combined into a new substance, like other uniform mixtures of metals (alloys). (d) No. A mineral is a natural, solid substance found on the Earth with a fixed chemical composition. The ornament was made by people, and its make-up depends on how much of each metal the silversmith chose to mix, so it is not a mineral. A silver lump itself could be displayed.
s: (a) Says element and native mineral
(b) Finds 75%
(c) Says mixture, as the metals keep their properties and are not combined
(d) Rejects it using natural, found on the Earth and fixed chemical composition

questions.q:
A foundry in Jharkhand needs 60 kg of copper metal and can get it from one of two sites (illustrative figures). At Site A, every tonne of rock dug gives 3 kg of natural lumps that a lab shows are made only of copper atoms. At Site B, every tonne of rock dug gives 12 kg of a mineral that is a compound of copper with other elements; one-third of the mineral's mass is copper, which must be extracted from it. Digging costs Rs 2,000 per tonne at either site, and extracting copper from the Site B mineral costs Rs 500 per kg of copper.
(a) What kind of mineral is found at Site A, and why does its copper need no extraction?
(b) Why can the copper at Site B not be obtained just by grinding and sieving the mineral?
(c) How many tonnes of rock must be dug at each site to get 60 kg of copper?
(d) Find the total cost of getting 60 kg of copper from each site.
(e) Which site should the foundry choose? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) A native mineral: the lumps are made only of copper atoms, so they are already the pure element copper and nothing has to be extracted. (b) The Site B mineral is a compound, and the elements of a compound cannot be separated by any physical method such as grinding or sieving. (c) Site A: 60 / 3 = 20 tonnes. Site B: each tonne gives 12 / 3 = 4 kg of copper, so 60 / 4 = 15 tonnes. (d) Site A: 20 x 2,000 = Rs 40,000. Site B: 15 x 2,000 = Rs 30,000 for digging plus 60 x 500 = Rs 30,000 for extraction, a total of Rs 60,000. (e) Site A. It needs 5 tonnes more rock dug, but because its copper is a native element and needs no extraction, it costs Rs 40,000 against Rs 60,000, which is Rs 20,000 less.
s: (a) Says native mineral, already the pure element copper
(b) Says the mineral is a compound, whose elements cannot be separated by physical methods
(c) Finds 20 tonnes for Site A and 15 tonnes for Site B
(d) Finds Rs 40,000 for Site A and Rs 60,000 for Site B
(e) Chooses Site A as Rs 20,000 cheaper despite more rock dug, because no extraction is needed
